newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Accused in Rwanda genocide trial questions witness.
newsitem.headline: Accused in Rwanda genocide trial questions witness.

text.p: The U.N. tribunal on Rwanda on Monday heard an ethnic Hutu mayor accused of genocide directly cross-examine a prosecution witness who said she watched him order the slaughter of Tutsis in his commune.

Jean-Paul Akayesu, the former mayor of Rwanda's Taba commune, pointedly tried to undermine the credibility of a Tutsi prosecution witness who told the court that he had personally ordered eight Tutsis hacked to death, legal experts said.

The cross-examination started after presiding Judge Laity Kama granted a request by Akayesu, 43, to personally take charge of defence questions to the first witness to appear before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR).
The court decision provoked a direct confrontation between Akayesu and his former employee, an accountant at Taba commune known to the court only as witness "K" to protect her identity.
Akayesu opened his cross-examination by saying :"Madam, I would like to wish you my best wishes for the year of 1997...I am very happy and proud to see you again."
"I wish you the same sir," Witness K replied.
Akayesu has pleaded not guilty to charges of genocide and crimes against humanity. If convicted he faces life imprisonment -- the tribunal's highest penalty.

Witness K told the court in three hours of testimony on Friday she watched Akayesu order a group of eight Tutsis hacked to death in front of his office on April 19, 1994 before telling Hutus to kill the commune's Tutsis.

She also said Akayesu imprisoned her for hours and threatened to kill her unless she provided information on the whereabouts of other Tutsis. He then relented saying he did not want a woman's blood on his hands, she added.
Akayesu started cross-examination in French from behind a screen flanked by two security guards while Witness K, who speaks Kinyarwanda, replied through an interpreter.

Akayesu's questions centred on events prior to the start of killings in Taba. He tried to show the witness knew little about the commune and that he was answerable to other local authorities and did not hold absolute power, legal experts said.
The cross-examination led to frequent interruptions from judge Kama and the three-person panel of judges demanding clarifications from both Akayesu and Witness K.
Akayesu, wearing a dark suit, appeared at ease with the process and repeatedly interrupted both Witness K and Judge Kama.
He is the first suspect to be tried before the tribunal for crimes between April and June 1994, when an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed.
The slow-moving process has been accompanied by allegations of mismanagement and abuses by the Arusha-based court. U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has promised decisive action to clean it up.
The trial was adjourned to Tuesday after Akayesu requested more time to prepare the next stage of his cross-examination.
Kama said a separate request by Akayesu to dismiss his two defence lawyers, who remained silent throughout the Monday proceedings, would be considered at the end of the week.
